extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in mathematics and the math research community
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the norms, standards, and expectations the mathematical community uses to judge proofs, authorship, priority, publication, and prize eligibility. Covers both technical and ethical criteria as described in a long-form article about the Poincaré conjecture and the Perelman controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a mathematical proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof begins with axioms or accepted truths and employs a sequence of logical statements to arrive at a conclusion; if the logic is watertight the result is a theorem. Unlike proofs in law or empirical science, a mathematical proof is definitive once correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments about a proof’s accuracy are mediated by the community and by peer-reviewed publication; a formally correct proof is expected to be conclusive rather than probabilistic or provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication implies completeness, correctness, and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication in a peer-reviewed journal is taken to imply that a proof has been checked and found to be complete, correct, and original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because publication confers these claims, the selection of reviewers and the integrity of the review process are important safeguards; lack of publication leaves a proof in a provisional state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review process standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers for mathematical results are supposed to be carefully chosen by journal editors, and the identity of an author under consideration is kept secret to insure fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This confidentiality and editorial selection are presented as essential to fair evaluation; deviation from careful reviewer selection or transparency about referee reports undermines confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fields Medal eligibility and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fields Medal is awarded every four years to between two and four mathematicians, and is given only to mathematicians aged forty and younger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The medal is intended both to reward past achievements and to stimulate future research; age eligibility is integral to its purpose of encouraging future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clay Millennium Prize eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for the Clay Mathematics Institute's million-dollar prize, a claimed solution must be published in a peer-reviewed venue and withstand two years of scrutiny by the mathematical community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates an explicit procedural requirement: publication plus extended community vetting (two years) before the prize can be awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between a mathematical gap and a gap in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A true mathematical gap consists of a missing or mistaken argument; a gap of exposition consists of omitted or compressed steps that an expert could expand. Only true gaps (missing or incorrect arguments) justify claiming an original result based on filling them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when Wiles had a gap it made the problem fair game until he fixed it; by contrast, if implicit steps can be made explicit by an expert, the proof is considered complete and the 'gap' is one of exposition, not novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to claim credit / originality
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two accepted ways to claim credit in mathematics: (1) produce an original proof; or (2) identify a significant (mathematical) gap in someone else’s proof and supply the missing argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filling in merely expository shortcuts does not count as originality. Claims based on alleged gaps should identify true mathematical deficiencies, not just exposition difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for clarity and completeness of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be sufficiently explicit to allow verification; extreme brevity or heavy use of shorthand that compresses many logical steps can make a proof vulnerable to challenge because many readers lack the specialized expertise to fill gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While concise presentation is acceptable, overly compressed arguments invite reconstruction projects by other teams and can slow community acceptance; exposition that includes irrelevant elegant results is also noted as atypical but not disqualifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community verification and consensus process
rubrics_metrics.description: Major proofs are vetted by experts through lectures, seminars, workshops, and explicit explications by teams who retrace and elaborate the original arguments; consensus about correctness emerges after detailed vetting by multiple experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until such vetting and consensus occur, claims should be treated with skepticism; teams sometimes produce long expository works or books to guide broader verification (examples: Tian & Morgan, Michigan group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms and risks of posting proofs on preprint servers / the internet
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting a proof on arXiv or the internet is a legitimate way to disseminate work but is unorthodox for claims of extremely famous problems because it bypasses traditional pre-publication vetting and carries the risk that errors will be public and others may appropriate or refine the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mathematicians view posting as risky or unconventional, but others (and some authors) see it as acceptable and even desirable; regardless, internet posting does not replace peer-reviewed publication for formal acceptance or prize eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for authorship, acknowledgement, and credit attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical profession expects stringent, explicit acknowledgement of prior contributions and careful attribution of originality; claiming credit without identifying concrete mathematical contributions or gaps is ethically problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include claiming a 'first complete proof' while describing others' work only in passing or failing to identify specific mathematical differences. Disputes (e.g., Yau/Givental, Yau/Tian) arise when these norms are perceived to be violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal editorial best practices (procedural transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial boards and editors are expected to follow transparent procedures—sharing manuscripts with board members, providing referee reports, and allowing time for comment—especially for significant or controversial papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: sending board members a terse email with three days to comment, or accepting a long, important paper without sharing referees’ reports or a copy of the paper; such behavior undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical norm: minimize politics, power, and control in credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians (as quoted in the article) assert that politics, power struggles, and attempts to control credit have no legitimate role and threaten the integrity of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The community values honest sharing of ideas and fair attribution; behavior perceived as leveraging institutional influence, national pride, or personal power to claim undeserved credit is condemned and harmful to the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a significant contribution when explicating another's proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Reworking or expanding someone's proof can be valuable when it provides genuine new approaches or resolves previously unsolvable technical points; merely rephrasing or making implicit steps explicit (without introducing new methods) is not normally treated as a new mathematical contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of significant contribution should specify which arguments are new or which essential steps were substituted by genuinely different approaches; broad statements of 'substituting several key arguments' without specificity invite dispute.
